headline: Penfield Reopens on the Ebb: Tautog to 6 Pounds, Porgies Stacked on the Cows
subhead: July 1 flipped the switch on blackfish season, and the timing couldn't be better with the water running warm from Greenwich to Bridgeport.
body_markdown:
Every July I run the same math in my head before I leave the dock: which piece of structure is going to be quiet enough to fish, and which tide window gets me there before the weekend armada shows up. Saturday I had two options — Penfield Reef on the last two hours of the ebb, or Cockenoe with a fluke drift on the incoming. Penfield won, and it wasn't close, because blackfish season flipped open July 1 and nobody east of Fairfield seems to have noticed yet.

That's the thing about Penfield this time of year — the rockpile off the lighthouse in 15 to 22 feet doesn't get hammered like it does in October when every boat out of Black Rock knows the drill. Right now it's just a handful of us who remember tautog opens back up mid-summer, and that's exactly the edge you want. I anchored up-current on the ebb, let the boat settle over the eastern boulder field, and started working green crabs on a 2-ounce jig head, snugged right into the pockets between the rocks. First fish came at 20 minutes in, a stout 4-pounder that buried the rod tip before I'd even felt the bite develop. By the time the tide laid out I had three keepers in the box, biggest going just under 6, and released a handful of shorts that were clearly feeling the same seasonal switch flip. The pattern held true to form — blackfish want that last third of the ebb when the current's dying down enough to hold bottom without a war-and-peace amount of lead, but still moving enough to keep bait working in the cracks. Slack water shuts it off almost like a valve.

While I was on tog, the Cows were doing exactly what they do every July — porgies stacked thick over the mussel beds in 18 to 25 feet. Guys anchoring up on the sandy edges around the rockpiles with squid strips and clam bellies on high-low rigs are filling coolers without much finesse required. It's not technical fishing, it's volume fishing, and right now the volume is there. Best window's been the two hours either side of high tide when the current slackens enough that you're not constantly re-baiting into a sweep. I'd rate the porgy bite as the most reliable thing happening in the western Sound right now — no asterisks, no qualifiers.

Fluke is the mixed bag this week. Cockenoe Reef and the sandy cuts around the Norwalk Islands are producing, but it's been feast-or-famine depending on which drift you land on. I worked three drifts off the southwest corner of Cockenoe on Thursday — first drift, nothing. Second drift, three keepers including a fat 4-pounder that ate a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a ¾-ounce bucktail like it hadn't eaten all week. Third drift, dead again. That's fluke fishing on structure — you're hunting for the exact seam where the sand meets the rock edge, and when you find it the bite turns on fast, but drift ten yards off it and you're wasting bait. Kings Point is reading 71.2 degrees right now, which is plenty warm to keep bait and fluke both active through the western Sound, and that thermal edge is part of why this zone is outproducing water further east — New London's still sitting in the mid-60s, a different ballgame entirely.

Striped bass have gone into the typical mid-summer pattern — daytime's tough, especially with boat traffic churning the Norwalk Islands into a washing machine every weekend. If you want bass right now, you fish the edges of the day. I had a solid hour at first light off Sheffield Island last week, live bunker on a fish-finder rig worked along the channel edge where the current funnels between the islands, and connected on two schoolies and one just-shy-of-slot fish that made the trip worth setting the alarm for. After 8 a.m. it was pleasure boats wall to wall and the bite simply shut down — not because the fish left, but because there's no such thing as a quiet drift through there once the weekenders are up and running. Same story off Greenwich Point — early morning bluefish have been showing up chasing bait pods along the flats, blitzes lasting maybe twenty minutes before they push off, so if you see the birds working, don't wait to see if it holds. Get a metal on — a Kastmaster or a diamond jig — and get it in the water immediately.

Heading into this coming week, I'd play the tide windows the same way I did Saturday. Blackfish on Penfield during the back half of the ebb, before the moon swings toward full and the current gets stronger than the bite can handle. Porgies on the Cows around high water, any day, boat traffic or not — they don't care. Fluke I'd treat as a hunt, not a certainty — hit Cockenoe or the Norwalk Islands sand pockets on a moving tide and be willing to make three or four drifts before committing. And for bass and blues, first light is the whole game right now — get out before the mooring fields wake up, because once the wakes start crossing the islands, the bite closes up shop until evening. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, I'd expect the western end to keep holding the warmer, more active water — which means Greenwich to Bridgeport keeps being the better bet over the cooler stretch east toward New Haven.
